title: Books to use
hook: books bought for show are furniture; buy what you'll read (On Tranquility 9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: less to lose, Diogenes letting his runaway servant go. Your line was less to lose. Did you find the thing that sets off the alarm? Day five hundred.

Day five hundred. Five hundred mornings, or nights, or lunch breaks. Some of you missed plenty and came back, which counts. Now picture a bookshelf. Maybe yours. How many of those books have you actually read? And how many are there partly because of how they look: to a guest, on a video call, to the person you hoped to become when you bought them? No shame. Seneca's Rome had the same habit, at a much grander scale. In chapter nine of On Tranquility, right after money, he turns to the one expense everyone thinks is above criticism. Books. Today: books to use.
screen: `DAY FIVE HUNDRED.` → `HOW MANY HAVE YOU READ?` → `THE EXPENSE ABOVE CRITICISM.`

segments.voice: First, even good spending has a limit. Spending on study, Seneca says, is the most honorable kind, but it's only reasonable within measure. What's the use of countless books and libraries whose owner can barely read the titles in a lifetime? A heap of books weighs on a learner; it doesn't teach. Better to give yourself to a few writers than to wander among many. Second, the great fire. Seneca brings up the library at Alexandria, where, he says, forty thousand books burned. The historian Livy had called that library a splendid monument to the taste and care of kings. Seneca disagrees, sharply. It wasn't taste and it wasn't care. It was studiosa luxuria, learned luxury. And then he takes even that back: not learned, since it was gathered for show, not for study. Third, books as furniture. He describes rich Romans who couldn't read well, whose dining rooms were lined with shelves to the ceiling, the book rolls valued for their handsome cases and labels. Among the baths and the fine furniture, Seneca says, a library had become one more thing a house was expected to have. Fourth, the point for us. Seneca isn't against books. He wrote shelves of them. He's against the gap between having and using, which by now you'll recognize: rich in enough, under the gold, mind the gap. A book you read twice is worth more to you than fifty you own.
screen: `EVEN STUDY SPENDING NEEDS MEASURE.` · `ALEXANDRIA: LEARNED LUXURY.` · `SHELVES TO THE DINING-ROOM CEILING.` · `HAVING VERSUS USING.` · then, large: `READ, DON'T DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Picture your shelf, or your e-reader, or your saved articles. Let your eye travel along it. Find one book you bought for a real reason and never opened, or opened and set down. Remember why you wanted it. What were you hoping it would give you? Now picture actually opening it tonight: the first page, the chair, the light. Not to finish it. Just to use it, for twenty minutes, like a tool you finally picked up. The bell holds the time.
Books to use. Seneca's warning in On Tranquility: books gathered for show are furniture, even at Alexandria. Give yourself to a few, and read them. Today's word.
Your line: read, don't display. Take one shelf book down today and read twenty minutes of it. Day five hundred.

howItsDone: Readers following Seneca often read a few books deeply instead of collecting many, and choose books for use rather than display.

fork.setup: Livy calls the great library at Alexandria a monument to royal taste and care. what does Seneca say?
options: he agrees and mourns its loss.
it was learned luxury, gathered for show.
fork.reveal: he calls it studiosa luxuria, learned luxury, then says not even learned, since it was gathered for show.

original.note: Latin, 'learned luxury': Seneca's verdict on a library gathered for show.

trapdoor: what you thought: owning books makes you learned.
what it means: Seneca says books gathered for show are furniture; a few, really read, teach.
what a scholar hears: Seneca's figure for the books burned at Alexandria varies in manuscripts (forty thousand or four hundred thousand), and the fire is usually tied to Caesar's war there in 48 BC.

notes: On Tranquility 9.4–7 paraphrased: spending on studies reasonable only within measure; the burden of many books; forty thousand books burned at Alexandria; Livy's praise ('elegantiae regum curaeque'); Seneca's 'studiosa luxuria', then 'not even studiosa'; ignorant owners with libraries as dining-room ornaments. Confirm.
